19. **The living map.** (added 29 October 2026) the owner: "In time I want environmental effects, seasons reflected on the map. Characters, armies, fighting shown, etc. Everything you can think of, which makes it a better game for a player or viewer. But I don't believe the time for these effects are quiet yet." With every feature built, the map's look becomes a blend of Imperator: Rome's map and a museum map of the Bronze Age world ("The map in true geography, and its look in time" under Interface): the environment and the seasons on the map, characters, armies and battles as they travel and fight, every unit and figure drawn after the period's own relics in its culture's idiom, a map that remembers the war, life drawn from the simulation, every level of what is built (roads by quality, harbours and docks, walls, water works, granaries, mines), a seasonal year, each realm's own map drawn by its scribes, omens in the margin and small scenes at big moments, and whatever else makes the game better to play or to watch, each measured on a throttled phone. Presentation only, with no change to rules, numbers or balance, so it may run beside item 18. **Stop for review.** Then **19+, answers to 19's review** (30 October 2026; the owner: "Yes to all"): each realm's own map pressed in clay for every court that writes cuneiform, as the period's clay maps were, and on papyrus for Egypt; a sacked city stays in ruins until its people come back, and they come back by the rule that already moves them ("Feeding a province draws its people": settled people move towards more room, measured in food, and the loose drift towards richer land), so the ruins fade as its people return and its walls are rebuilt with item 15's works, with no rule for rebuilding (the owner: "no special rules for cities recovering, people will migrate back at the harvest potential difference there becomes bigger than neighboring cities"); and Egypt's view gets hieratic notes as decoration only, the map's own text staying in the reader's language. Presentation only. Then **19++, the visual pass** (30 October 2026; the owner: "I also think amarna letters needs another visual pass. With the instructions to make it as visually impressive as it possibly can, without tanking the performance."): every screen, not only the map, made as impressive as it can be: the map at every zoom, the province card, the seat view, the letters and their tablets, the council, the chronicle, replay and god view, menus and the first screen, in light and dark, on phone and desktop. One look throughout, in the style the living map set (Imperator: Rome's map and a museum map of the Bronze Age, each culture drawn in its own idiom after the period's relics), with type, colour, texture, light, motion and the small touches that make a game feel crafted, never clutter that hides what a king needs to read. The bound is that it stays playable on a phone (the owner: "Well, it can get slower, but must be playable on a phone. That's the criteria."): measured as item 19 measures it, on a throttled phone in the busiest scene of each screen, smooth enough to read and play and to watch at top speed without falling behind, with reduced motion respected; it may cost more than now where it buys something worth seeing. The pass starts by finding every graphical glitch and inconsistency on every screen (the owner: "There are also many graphical glitches and Inconsistencies in the game right now."): things drawn wrong, out of place, overlapping or flickering, and the same thing drawn or named differently in two places; each is listed in the PR with its picture and fixed. The PR shows every screen before and after at 390 px and desktop 2x, light and dark, with the performance numbers before and after. It also makes the main map carry all it can paint without clutter, and builds the map's views for every system already in the game (Interface, "The main map and its views"; the owner, 31 October 2026: "Agreed to all. Expertly!"); from then on each new system brings its own view in the item that builds it. Cities, said outright (the owner, 31 October 2026: "We already have queued in the graphic update that we should see real cities, and see them grow and decline with population, right? and all buildings one can build around?", then "Yes, expertly to all!"): each city is drawn as the city it is, in its own culture's style after the period's relics, sized by its people, growing and shrinking as they come and go, and every level of what is built in and around it shows as one zooms in ("Every level of what is built shows" in "The look, in time"). Presentation only, so it may run beside item 18. Then **19+++, the music** (30 October 2026; the owner: "Would love if we could make something properly similar in that style instead (choir, strings, reed and drums) around the Hurrian Hymn, that actually sounds good. \[...\] And have the music be dynamic exactly like it is in Empire Earth. \[...\] the music is same for all you play, but should be dynamic in the same way as Empire Earth, with the few variations on the pieces, and each piece playing according to the situation. Use the Empire Earth pieces as the template, and make as many as Empire Earth had, each inspired by each piece there, expertly."). The game has no music or sound yet. First the template: list Empire Earth's pieces from its sources, how many there are, the mood and role of each and when the game played it, and how its dynamic music chose and changed pieces with the situation. Then as many pieces of our own, one for each of Empire Earth's, each taking that piece's role, mood, pace and colour (a solemn choir, warm strings, a solo reed, frame drums and the period's lyres, harps and pipes) and nothing that is that piece's own: no melody, no recognisable progression or line, since those belong to their owners; the melodies come from the Hurrian Hymn of Ugarit (about 1400 BCE, free to use, read from its scholarly reconstructions) and from new themes in the Babylonian tunings, so the game has one musical voice, the same for every court. Each piece has a few variations, and the music is dynamic as Empire Earth's was: the situation of the seat being played (or the whole map in god view) picks the piece, calm, rising tension, war, siege, battle, triumph, loss and the age's last seasons, changing at a phrase's end, never the same variation twice running. Some of each piece's variations are the same piece in a darker or a brighter mode of the Babylonian tunings: the music chooses the darker as the situation worsens and the brighter as it improves, so the mood turns within a piece between the changes of piece, at no cost in files. It must sound good, not merely correct: composed as scores, rendered offline with orchestral and choir samples whose licences allow their rendered sound in a free, open game (CC0 or as free, each licence recorded), mixed and mastered to one loudness, and shipped as compressed audio loaded on demand so the first screen stays fast and the phone stays playable. And a sound design in the manner of Crusader Kings II (the owner, 30 October 2026: "And sound effect can be inspired by CK2?", then, to the design session's take, "Yes, please, expertly!"), its approach and feel, nothing from its files: every action and event has its own short sound in the period's terms, so a player hears what happened without looking (the stylus pressed into clay as a letter is written, a cylinder seal rolled, a tablet set in its envelope, gold weighed on the scales, a courier's arrival, Egypt's trumpets or a war horn when war is declared, the sistrum for a temple or an omen, a lyre's phrase when an envoy is received); restrained, short and soft, each with a few slight variations so it never tires; a quiet bed of the world under the music that follows what the map shows (the Nile's water, the steppe's wind, a city's market, a siege camp); and a short sting for the great moments (a capital falling, a king's death, the age's end) before the music takes them up. Three layers, the music leading (decided 1 November 2026; the owner, 1 November 2026: "It plays dozens of sound effects at any one time. I believe ck2 only played many of those soundeffects if they happen to you", then "Yes, in ck2, you get environmental sounds. Like a plague in a county, you zoom in, you get the moaning and commotion. You zoom in on a battle, you hear the steel clash. But all the event stuff is for players only, or if you spectate a player, you hear specifically what they hear"): the music; the world's sounds, where things happen on the map (a battle's clash, a siege, a plague's moaning and commotion, a storm, a market, the wind), heard only near the view when zoomed in, softer with distance, and the same for every viewer, a spectator included, but only of what that viewer's seat knows; and the event sounds, for one seat only: its own clicks and what happens to its realm (its letters, envoys, armies, provinces), heard by its player, or by a spectator watching through that seat, never in god view. The world's sounds and the events add layers under the music, never drown it: mixed below it, never sudden or loud, and capped (at most two or three event sounds at once, none repeated within a few seconds), so the fix is in how the soundscape is chosen and mixed, not in the sounds themselves. And nothing heard ever reveals what lies beyond the fog of war (the owner, 1 November 2026: "Important! The music must never reveal what's outside the fog of war. Remember, a king only sees what's within a season at any one time."): the mood, its darker or brighter shade, the stings, the great moments, the world's sounds and the event sounds all follow only what the seat knows as it learns it, its own sight and the news that has reached it, never the true map; a battle or a fall the seat has not heard of plays nothing, even with the view zoomed in on it, and its sting comes, if at all, when the news arrives; and what the record lacks counts as unknown, never as seen. What a seat hears is what its own map shows (the owner, 1 November 2026: "But of course, you know where a sea is, so some things you can zoom in on and hear, without it revealing anything. Because these are static. And if you zoom in on a city that is really burned but that you still believe is buzzing, then it should probably play the urban commotion sound?"): the land itself, seas, rivers, deserts and the wind, never changes and is known to all, so it is heard anywhere the view goes; and a place sounds as the seat last knew it, so a city burned seasons ago that the seat still believes thriving plays its market's bustle until the news of its burning arrives, and then its ruin, as the map's dated knowledge already shows it ("Fog of war as a gradient"). Only god view hears the true map. A test proves it: a hidden battle, siege or fall changes nothing a seat hears. On by default at a regular volume, never blasting at start-up: the first music fades in over the opening seconds rather than starting at full, unlike the main theme that opened Crusader Kings II at full volume (the owner, 1 November 2026, answering the music lane's question: "Agreed. Keep them on, regular volume, but don't blast someone when they start up, like say CK2, even though the main theme there was epice. SO i didn't really mind."), with music and sound switches and their levels remembered between visits. The owner judges by ear: the PR has a listening page with every piece and variation, and the template's list beside it; any piece he dislikes is redone before it merges. Presentation only. Its sounds are built on the season's stream of events (items 17a and 17+++): marching, the clash of battle, wind and waves, weather, an avalanche's thunder, each placed on the map, so that zoomed in near a unit you hear it, louder the nearer, and zoomed out you hear the world's bed and the great moments (the owner, 31 October 2026: "If you are zoomed in near a unit in the waves, I want to hear it."). And a fallback, built alongside the Empire Earth pieces rather than after them, in case the Empire Earth style does not come out well by the owner's ear (31 October 2026: "I however, has always also liked the main theme of the original Civilization. You know the 8-bit version of it that was the original game, not the Civ4 version. So maybe that style will be easier to emulate, if Empire Earth don't work out well right now.", then "Yes, and I would like both options."): the original Civilization's method, short synthesised themes, a few for each court, around the Hurrian Hymn, made in the browser's own sound engine with no samples, in two versions for him to choose between on hearing: one in period timbres (a synthesised lyre, reed pipe, frame drum and sistrum) and one in pure 8-bit, as the 1991 game sounded. Both versions play one score, in the period's own tunings (the owner, 31 October 2026, to the design session's two recommendations: "I like option a for both, as you recommend. We will try it expertly, and see how it is in practive!"). The pieces are written once, as notes, layers and the cues that switch them, and each version plays them with its own arrangement rules: the 8-bit version spreads held chords into arpeggios and echoes, and the period version lets notes ring with looser timing. That is the 1991 game's own way, since its one score played through whichever sound card a player had. The scales are the Babylonian lyre tunings of the tablets from Nippur and Ur, seven modes. Each court has a home mode, as presentation only, and the situation shifts the mode, darker in war or mourning and back again at a feast, so the mood is heard as well as the piece. Ugarit's theme is the Hurrian Hymn, itself written in one of those modes, played from one scholarly reconstruction that the listening page names. Egypt's mode is a reading, since how its harps were tuned is unknown. The owner judges the result by ear. The same playback, layers, placement on the map and hearing by zoom serve every version, so only the pieces change; the listening page gives each version side by side, the Empire Earth pieces and both of the fallback's versions, so the owner hears all three in one sitting and chooses (the owner, 31 October 2026, to building the fallback alongside and to the mode variations in the Empire Earth pieces: "I say yes, expertly, to both."). Empire Earth's style, with The Sims and Deus Ex, is kept for the owner's next game if it does not land here.

    Then **19+++b, the music follows the state** (decided 9 November 2026, archive item 241): the music follows the seat's state, not each season's events, as Civilization V's and Empire Earth's music does, since a watched season passes in under two seconds and the sounds and stings already carry the events. A heat picks the mood: raised by what the seat knows (much by its own army in a real battle or its land besieged, some by foreign troops in its land, little by a skirmish with a city-state), cooling with time counted in both seasons and seconds, whichever is slower, so the music feels the same watched at speed and played a season at a time; each mood has a higher threshold to enter than to leave. It rises fast and falls slow: a rise crosses at the next phrase end, within about 8 s; a fall never cuts a piece, which plays to its end and rests before the calmer music comes, one step down at a time (battle, war, tension, calm). A mood holds at least about 90 s of play, unless the seat's own capital is attacked. Battle music is earned: a sizeable battle of the seat's own men, one against a Great King, or one in its own land; smaller fights bring their drums and at most war. The darker or brighter shade chooses the next piece's variation and never cuts the one playing. God view hears one realm, and no mood is a switch (19+++c). Measured in script games, for a seat and in god view at each speed: the mood's changes a minute and the share of time in each, with a first guess of about one change in two minutes, then tuned by the owner's ear. No piece is recomposed. Presentation only.

    Then **19+++c, war music a share, never the whole** (decided 10 November 2026, archive item 247): the music is mostly the game's calm and its age, with war heard when it is the listener's own, as in Civilization V and VI, Crusader Kings II and Europa Universalis IV, where the music follows one country and war only weighs on it. A spectator hears what he chose to watch, as in the spectator modes of Civilization VI and Paradox's games (archive items 248 and 249): a realm he watches, that realm's heat in its music; a character he follows, that character's own (his battles, his danger, his captivity) in his realm's music; and drifting over the whole world, the world's own heat, raised by what changes the world (a great battle between Great Kings, a Great King's capital newly besieged or taken, a Great King captive or fallen), little by a siege that drags on or by the city-states' wars, in the music of whichever realm is doing the most at that moment, kept until another clearly does more. Never the middle of the view, which pans fast and, zoomed out, shows no more than the rest. A spectator's music turns over calmly, as Civilization's does: a change of what he watches never cuts a piece, which plays on to its end, or at most about 45 s to a phrase end, before the next is drawn for what he now watches; it rises at once only for something clear in front of him (a battle of the realm or character he watches, that realm's capital attacked), and the world's own heat changes the music only at a piece's end. A player at his seat keeps 19+++b's clearer triggers. The world's wars still sound in their stings. No mood is a switch: each next piece is drawn by chance from the pieces of every mood, weighted toward the mood's own, as Paradox's games weigh each song by the country's state: in war about one piece in two is a war piece, in tension one in three, the rest tension or calm. A rise is heard at once, the 90-second hold of 19+++b holding back falls only: the piece that crosses on it is the new mood's own, and the draw weighs the pieces after it; battle music stays earned, one piece at a time. A siege heats less after its first few seasons. Rests of silence, a few seconds to half a minute, fall between pieces, so the world's own sounds come through. First guesses, measured as in 19+++b and tuned by the owner's ear: the war family under a third of god view, and under half of a seat's play while it is at war. No piece is recomposed. Presentation only.
